paragraphs.text: Every autumn, a surprising variety of animals prepare to disappear. Bears retreat into dens, ground squirrels seal themselves into burrows, and certain bats cluster in caves where the temperature remains cold but steady. For weeks or months they will barely move, eat nothing and, in many cases, allow their bodies to cool to temperatures that would kill a human within hours. Hibernation has long been described as a kind of deep sleep, but research over the past few decades has shown that it is something quite different, and in some ways far stranger. The animals that do it are not closely related, which suggests that the ability has evolved several times; some species prepare for months, while others can enter the state within days.
paragraphs.label: A

paragraphs.text: The basic purpose is to save energy. Keeping a body warm in cold weather requires large amounts of fuel, and in winter food is scarce. By lowering its body temperature and slowing its metabolism, a hibernating animal can survive on fat stored during the autumn. The savings are dramatic: a hibernating ground squirrel may reduce its energy use to a few per cent of its normal level, and its heart may beat only a handful of times a minute instead of several hundred. Some small species allow their body temperature to fall to just above freezing. Fat reserves built up in late summer can amount to a large share of body weight.
paragraphs.label: B

paragraphs.text: Hibernation is not a single continuous state. Most small hibernators periodically rewarm themselves, returning to normal body temperature for less than a day before cooling down again, and they repeat this cycle every one to three weeks throughout the winter. These arousals are extremely expensive, consuming most of the energy used during the entire season, and their purpose is still debated. One explanation is that the animals need to restore functions that shut down at low temperatures, such as parts of the immune system; another is that they need to sleep, since true sleep appears to be impossible at very low body temperatures. Arousals are also risky, because a sudden rise in temperature puts great strain on the heart. The rewarming is driven by a special kind of fat that produces heat directly.
paragraphs.label: C

paragraphs.text: Bears behave differently from small hibernators. Their body temperature falls only a few degrees, and they can wake relatively quickly if disturbed, which led some researchers to question whether they truly hibernate at all. Yet their metabolism drops almost as much as that of smaller species, and they can go for several months without eating, drinking or passing waste. Female bears even give birth and nurse their young during this period, supporting the cubs entirely from their own stored reserves. Their stored fat is used so efficiently that they lose surprisingly little muscle during the winter.
paragraphs.label: D

paragraphs.text: What most interests medical researchers is how hibernators avoid damage that would be serious in other animals. A bear lying almost motionless for months loses very little bone or muscle, whereas a human confined to bed for a few weeks loses both rapidly. Hibernating squirrels survive a greatly reduced blood supply to the brain and then return to full activity without apparent harm. Blood that moves so slowly would normally form dangerous clots, yet hibernators seem to adjust their blood chemistry to prevent this. Hibernating animals also appear to recover from reduced oxygen supply in ways that would severely damage human tissue.
paragraphs.label: E

paragraphs.text: These abilities have prompted several lines of research. Scientists studying muscle loss are examining which genes are active in hibernating bears, hoping to find ways of protecting patients who must spend long periods in bed. Others are investigating whether a hibernation-like state could protect the brain after a stroke or allow organs to be stored for longer before transplantation. Space agencies have also shown interest in the idea that astronauts might one day be placed in a state of reduced metabolism for long journeys, although this remains highly speculative. Some of this work has already identified proteins that may help to preserve muscle.
paragraphs.label: F

paragraphs.text: Climate change is already affecting hibernating animals. Warmer winters can cause some species to wake earlier or to hibernate for shorter periods, and animals that emerge before their food supply is available may struggle to survive. In some regions, marmots now end their hibernation weeks earlier than they did several decades ago. The consequences vary between species: some may benefit from a longer active season, while others face a growing mismatch between their own timing and that of the plants and insects on which they depend. Species living at high altitude may be particularly vulnerable, since they have little room to move to cooler areas.
paragraphs.label: G

paragraphs.text: The more hibernation is studied, the less it resembles the simple sleep that the word once suggested. It is an active, carefully regulated state in which the body is switched to a different mode of operation, able to tolerate conditions that would otherwise be fatal. Understanding how that switch works remains one of the most intriguing problems in biology, and one whose answers may prove useful far beyond the dens and burrows where animals spend the winter. For now, the animals themselves remain far ahead of the scientists trying to copy them.
paragraphs.label: H

paragraphs.text: Adhesives are among the most widely used materials in the modern world and among the least noticed. Their market is worth tens of billions of dollars a year, yet few people think about them until they fail. They hold together the layers of plywood and cardboard, the soles of shoes, the components of phones and the wings of some aircraft. Yet despite their importance, the question of exactly why one surface sticks to another turned out to be surprisingly difficult to answer, and it has been answered in several different ways depending on the materials involved.
paragraphs.label: A

paragraphs.text: The oldest adhesives were natural. Archaeologists have found stone tools that were attached to wooden handles with tar made from birch bark more than two hundred thousand years ago, a process that required heating the bark carefully in the absence of air. Later, people boiled animal skins and bones to make glue, and used starch from plants, resins from trees and even the sticky secretions of insects. For thousands of years these materials were the only glues available, and animal glue remained standard in woodworking until well into the twentieth century. Some of these traditional glues are still preferred by restorers of old furniture and musical instruments, because they can be undone with heat and moisture.
paragraphs.label: B

paragraphs.text: Synthetic adhesives transformed the field in the twentieth century. Chemists developed glues based on plastics that set by chemical reaction rather than by drying, producing bonds that were stronger than the materials they joined and resistant to water and heat. Epoxy resins, which harden when two components are mixed, became essential in aircraft manufacturing, allowing panels to be joined without the rivets that weaken metal by making holes in it. Superglues, which set almost instantly on contact with the moisture present on most surfaces, followed in the 1950s. Hot-melt glues, applied as a liquid and hardening as they cool, are now widely used in packaging and bookbinding. Many modern cars also contain dozens of metres of adhesive in their bodies, replacing welds in places where different materials meet.
paragraphs.label: C

paragraphs.text: The science of why these substances stick involves several different mechanisms. Some adhesives flow into tiny irregularities in a surface and lock into place as they harden, a mechanical grip that works best on rough or porous materials such as wood. Others form chemical bonds with the surface itself. Nearly all rely to some extent on very weak attractions between molecules that are extremely close together, forces that are negligible over large distances but become significant when two materials are in intimate contact over a large area. Engineers often combine two or more of these mechanisms in a single joint, and preparing the surface, by cleaning or roughening it, is often more important than the choice of adhesive.
paragraphs.label: D

paragraphs.text: Those weak forces explain one of the most remarkable examples of adhesion in nature. Geckos can run up glass walls and hang from ceilings by a single toe, yet their feet are dry and leave no residue. Each toe is covered with millions of microscopic hairs, which divide into even finer tips, and the enormous number of contact points means that the weak attractions between molecules add up to a considerable force. Because the hairs are angled, the gecko can detach its foot simply by changing the angle at which it pulls. A gecko can stick and unstick its feet several times a second while running.
paragraphs.label: E

paragraphs.text: Engineers have tried to copy the gecko for decades. Laboratory versions made of tiny synthetic fibres can support substantial weights and be attached and removed many times, and some have been used in grippers for robots and in devices designed to grasp objects in space, where conventional suction cups cannot work. Making such materials cheaply and in large quantities has proved difficult, however, and most still lose their grip after repeated use, as dust and wear damage the fine fibres. Some versions have been tested on climbing robots designed to inspect buildings and bridges.
paragraphs.label: F

paragraphs.text: Another source of inspiration is found in the sea. Mussels attach themselves to rocks with threads that hold firm in wet, salty and turbulent conditions that defeat most synthetic glues. Researchers have identified the proteins responsible, which contain a particular chemical group that bonds strongly to wet surfaces, and have developed synthetic versions for use in surgery. Such adhesives could one day replace some stitches and staples, sealing wounds and tissues inside the body where ordinary glues fail. Mussel-inspired coatings are also being tested for ships, where they could resist the growth of marine organisms.
paragraphs.label: G

paragraphs.text: Adhesives also present environmental problems. Many products, from furniture to packaging, combine different materials glued so firmly together that they cannot be separated for recycling, and some glues release harmful chemicals as they cure. Researchers are now developing adhesives that hold firmly during use but can be released on demand, for example by heat or an electric current, so that products can be taken apart at the end of their lives. The challenge that once concerned engineers most, making things stick, is increasingly being matched by the challenge of making them come apart. Some manufacturers have begun to design products with disassembly in mind, and glue, in other words, has become part of the circular economy.
paragraphs.label: H

paragraphs.text: For most of the history of medicine, placebos were regarded as a nuisance. A placebo is a treatment with no active ingredient, such as a sugar pill, and its main role in modern medicine has been as a comparison in clinical trials: a new drug is judged effective only if it performs better than a placebo given to a similar group of patients. The improvements seen in patients receiving placebos were treated as noise to be subtracted. In recent decades, however, researchers have begun to ask whether the placebo effect might itself be put to use, and the question has divided doctors and ethicists. The shift reflects both new evidence and changing ideas about what patients should be told, and the reputation of the placebo has rarely been higher, or more contested.
paragraphs.label: A

paragraphs.text: The effect is real but easily misunderstood. Ellen Marsh, a psychologist who studies placebo responses, points out that much of the improvement seen in placebo groups is not caused by the placebo at all. Many conditions improve naturally over time, and patients often enter trials when their symptoms are at their worst, so some recovery would have occurred anyway. Once these factors are removed, genuine placebo effects remain, but they are largely confined to symptoms that the patient experiences, such as pain, nausea and fatigue, rather than to measurable changes in disease. Some placebo groups in trials of pain treatments improve almost as much as those receiving the drug.
paragraphs.label: B

paragraphs.text: Within those limits, the effects can be substantial. Studies have found that the expectation of relief can trigger the release of pain-relieving substances produced by the body itself, and that the context of treatment, including the manner of the doctor, the colour of a pill and even its price, can influence how much benefit patients report. Rafael Duarte, a physician, argues that doctors already use these effects without acknowledging it, whenever they reassure a patient or express confidence in a treatment, and that it would be better to study them openly than to rely on them informally. Even the way a treatment is described can matter: patients warned about possible side effects sometimes report them after taking a pill with no active ingredient. Surgery can also produce placebo effects, as some trials comparing real and sham operations have shown.
paragraphs.label: C

paragraphs.text: The main obstacle to using placebos deliberately has been ethical. Giving a patient a sugar pill while claiming that it contains a drug involves deception, and deceiving patients undermines the trust on which medicine depends. Nadia Kaur, a bioethicist, regards this as decisive: whatever the benefits, a doctor who lies to a patient violates the right of that patient to make informed decisions about their own treatment. For many years, this seemed to settle the matter, since it was assumed that a placebo could only work if the patient believed it was real. Professional codes in many countries forbid doctors to prescribe placebos deceptively.
paragraphs.label: D

paragraphs.text: That assumption has now been challenged. In a number of studies, patients with conditions such as chronic back pain and irritable bowel syndrome were given pills that they were told openly contained no active ingredient, along with an explanation of how placebo effects work. Many reported significant improvement compared with patients who received no pills at all. Kaur considers these open-label placebos ethically acceptable in principle, since nothing is concealed, although she remains uneasy about how the explanation offered to patients is framed. Some patients said that the ritual of taking a pill at regular times itself seemed to help.
paragraphs.label: E

paragraphs.text: Not everyone is persuaded. Tom Ashby, a pharmacologist, notes that most open-label studies have been small, relatively short and difficult to blind, since patients know which group they are in, and that some of the improvement may reflect the wish of patients to please the researchers. He argues that the evidence is promising but insufficient to justify routine use, and that resources would be better spent on establishing which features of the doctor-patient relationship produce benefit, since these could be used without any pill at all. He also points out that the improvements reported have usually been modest.
paragraphs.label: F

paragraphs.text: There are also practical concerns. If patients come to believe that a pill without a drug can relieve their symptoms, they might delay seeking treatment for a condition that requires it. Duarte acknowledges this risk but points out that placebos would be offered only after proper diagnosis, and only for conditions in which symptom relief is the main goal. Marsh adds that for some patients, particularly those with chronic pain who have gained little from conventional drugs, even a modest improvement without side effects would be valuable. Others worry that patients may feel dismissed if offered a pill with nothing in it.
paragraphs.label: G

paragraphs.text: The debate reflects a broader shift in how medicine understands the relationship between mind and body. The placebo effect is no longer regarded simply as an error to be controlled, but as evidence that expectations, attention and trust can influence how patients feel. Whether that knowledge is best applied through honest placebos or through better care and communication remains open, but the old view that placebos have nothing to offer except a baseline for comparison is increasingly difficult to defend. The question is no longer whether expectation matters, but how it should be used.
paragraphs.label: H
